figures.caption: Fig. 1. Workflow for the computational multiscale approach adopted in this research paper. The procedure starts with initial atomic structures used in first-principles calculations, DFT, and AIMD. The data generated from these calculations is used as a training set to develop a Deep Learning Potential for Machine Learning (ML) Molecular Dynamics. The ion transport parameters obtained from MD simulations are subsequently used to develop the continuum model. Finally, the results from both Machine Learning MD and the Continuum Model are analyzed to reach a coherent conclusion and provide recommendations. 2

Fig. 2. Ball and stick models of optimized bulk structures of a) LNTO, b)LGPS, and c) LCO; Red, blue, light green, dark green, tan, yellow, purple, and gray balls are oxygen (O), cobalt (Co), lithium (Li), niobium (Nb), tantalum (Ta), sulfur (S), germanium (Ge), and phosphorous (P) atoms, respectively; d) surface energies per unit area for 18 LNTO surfaces; Light blue bar shows the (131) surface with the lowest surface energy. (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.) 3

Fig. 3. Schematic of the workflow for developing a Deep Learning Potential (DLP) for Machine Learning Molecular Dynamics (MLMD). Atomic coordinates obtained from AIMD data are used as inputs to neural networks that predict atomic energies and forces for MLMD simulations. The embedding neural network generates descriptors from atomic coordinates and passes them to the fitting neural networks. The fitting neural networks output the atomic energy contributions, which are summed to obtain the total energy and corresponding forces. thickness of the passivating interphase layer on the LGPS side esti­ mated by the 1D continuum model was used to calculate the charge- transfer resistance at the cathode|solid-electrolyte (LCO|LGPS) interface. Distribution of lithium inside the LCO cathode was assumed to follow a solid solution mechanism, where mass transfer occurs through a diffusion process model

Fig. 4. DFT vs DLP energies (a) and forces (b–f) for atoms at the LCO|LGPS interface, i.e., cobalt (Co), germanium (Ge), lithium (Li), oxygen (O), and phosphorus (P). FDFT and EDFT are forces and energy, respectively, calculated from DFT-generated data. FDLP and EDLP are predicted forces and energy, respectively, generated using the DLP. A dashed 45◦line shows an ideal, perfect correlation between trained and predicted data. 5

Fig. 5. Equilibrium plots of temperature (T, K), kinetic energy (KE, eV), potential energy (PE, eV/atom), and pressure (P, bar/atom) for the Machine Learning Molecular Dynamics simulation. The simulation of the (001)LGPS|(010)LCO interface was performed for ~3 ns using a Deep Learning Potential. The thermodynamic properties begin to stabilize at approximately 2 ns, indicating the system approaches equilibrium beyond this time. 6

Fig. 6. Interdiffusion of Co atom into LGPS (a) NVT at 0 ns, (b) NVT at 1.5 ns, (c) NVT at 3 ns. Red, blue, green, yellow, purple, and gray balls are O, Co, Li, S, P, and Ge atoms, respectively. The red-blueish region represents LCO, and the green-yellowish region represents LGPS. The mixed region at the interface observed at 1.5 ns and 3 ns indicates ionic interdiffusion and intermixing, leading to the formation and growth of an interphase layer. The sharp interface at 10 s is shown by the dashed line, whereas the interdiffusion-induced diffused interphase obtained after 150 h is denoted by the solid black line. Fig. 9. Final trajectory structures of the LCO|LNTO interface at 2 ns with no Cobalt (blue) interdiffusion for the LCO surfaces a) (104), b) (010), c) (110). The blue- dominant region is LCO, while the red-orange region corresponds to LNTO. No ionic interdiffusion or intermixing is observed throughout the simulation, indicating that the structure remains stable over the entire trajectory. Fig. 10. (a) Distribution of lithium concentration within the LCO cathode close to the end of discharge at 0.1C rate. No variation in electrolyte salt concentration occurs within LGPS because it is a single-ion conducting solid electrolyte. (b) Distribution of hydrostatic stress within the LCO cathode and LGPS solid electrolyte as observed close to the end of discharge. The randomness in stress distribution observed within the LCO cathode can be attributed to the randomness in the orientation of the anisotropic grains.
